bib.title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier

question: How can the prediction of any classifier be explained faithfully and interpretably so that users can decide whether to trust a prediction or a model?
hypothesis: Locally faithful sparse linear explanations, plus a diverse set of representative explanations, help users judge trust, choose between models and improve untrustworthy classifiers.
contributions: LIME, an algorithm that can explain the predictions of any classifier or regressor in a faithful way, by approximating it locally with an interpretable model.
SP-LIME, a method that selects a set of representative instances with explanations to address the trusting the model problem, via submodular optimization.
Comprehensive evaluation with simulated and human subjects, measuring the impact of explanations on trust and associated tasks.

method.summary: LIME perturbs an interpretable binary representation of one instance (words or super-pixels), labels the perturbations with the black-box model, weights them by an exponential proximity kernel and fits a sparse linear model (K-LASSO feature selection then least squares). SP-LIME greedily picks B instances whose explanations cover the most globally important features. Evaluated with simulated users on sentiment data and with Mechanical Turk and graduate-student subjects.
method.task: Post-hoc explanation of classifier predictions (text and image)

datasets.name: Books and DVDs product reviews (Blitzer et al. 2007)
datasets.split: 1600 train / 400 test; for the model-selection experiment 80/20 train/validation split of the training data
datasets.preprocessing: bag of words; in 5.4 10 artificial noisy features added (each in 10% of examples of one class, 20% of the other on train/validation; 10% in each class on test)

datasets.name: 20 newsgroups, Christianity vs Atheism subset
datasets.split: original 20 newsgroups split; test accuracy 94.0% (original) and 88.6% (cleaned)
datasets.preprocessing: cleaned version has many non-generalising features manually removed

datasets.name: religion dataset (authors' own)
datasets.source: Atheism and Christianity websites from the DMOZ directory and human curated lists

datasets.name: Husky vs Wolf images
datasets.size: 20 training images, 60 additional test images, 10 shown to subjects
datasets.split: train 20 hand selected (all wolves with snow, huskies without)
datasets.preprocessing: features from first max-pooling layer of Inception

models.name: LIME (sparse linear explanation)
models.architecture: linear model g(z')=w_g.z' over binary interpretable representation

other.distance: cosine for text, L2 for images
other.selection: K-LASSO: Lasso regularisation path to select K features, then least squares

models.name: DT, LR (L2), NN, SVM RBF (bag of words), RF 1000 trees on average word2vec

other.use: pairs retrained until validation accuracy within 0.1% but test accuracy differs by at least 5%

inference.samples: N=15,000 perturbed samples in simulated experiments; N=5000 in the timing example; simulated trust results averaged over 100 runs; model-selection results over 800 runs; human studies 100 users per setting (6.2), 10 initial subjects then 5 per classifier per round for 3 rounds giving 250 classifiers (6.3), 27 subjects (6.4)

parameters.K: 10 in simulated experiments and image example; 6 in human choose-classifier study; 10 words in feature engineering
parameters.hyperparameters: parzen and LIME hyper-parameters set by cross validation; sigma value not stated
parameters.greedy_baseline: greedily remove features contributing most to predicted class until prediction changes or K features
parameters.pick: random pick (RP) or submodular pick (SP), greedy maximisation of weighted coverage, 1-1/e guarantee; text importance I_j=sqrt(sum_i |W_ij|)

other.cost: explaining RF with 1000 trees, N=5000, laptop, no GPU or parallelisation: under 3 seconds; Inception about 10 minutes per prediction

metrics.name: Recall of gold features
metrics.definition: fraction of the (at most 10) features used by an interpretable classifier that the explanation recovers, averaged over test instances

metrics.name: F1 of trustworthiness
metrics.definition: F1 on trustworthy predictions of a simulated user against an oracle that marks a prediction untrustworthy if it changes when untrustworthy features are removed

metrics.name: % correct choice
metrics.definition: share of runs or users that pick the classifier with higher real-world (test or religion set) accuracy

metrics.name: Real world accuracy
metrics.definition: accuracy on the religion dataset after feature removal

baselines: parzen (Baehrens et al. 2010 gradient of Parzen window global approximation)
eval.protocol: Simulated users on books and DVDs; MTurk subjects with basic knowledge of religion; graduate students with at least one graduate ML course for Husky vs Wolf, answers judged by 3 independent evaluators (majority). Significance p=0.01 stated for Table 1 only.

availability.data: code and data for replicating the experiments at the same URL

results.claim: Husky vs Wolf: subjects trusting the bad model fell after seeing explanations
results.setup: Logistic regression on Inception first max-pool features, trained on 20 hand-picked images; 10 test predictions (8 correct); graduate students with at least one ML course; before then after explanations
results.table: Table 2, row Trusted the bad model, column After

results.claim: Husky vs Wolf: subjects naming snow as a potential feature rose after explanations
results.table: Table 2, row Snow as a potential feature, column After
results.note: Before value 12 out of 27; authors say sample size is small

results.claim: Human subjects best chose the better classifier with LIME and submodular pick
results.setup: MTurk, 100 users per setting, K=B=6, SVM RBF on 20 newsgroups original vs cleaned; values read from Fig 9 bar labels
results.note: Figure 9 prints bar labels 68.0, 75.0, 80.0, 89.0 without a text mapping; mapping greedy RP 68, LIME RP 75, greedy SP 80, LIME SP 89 is by the figure legend order and was confirmed by an earlier render per the legacy report

results.claim: The original classifier looks better on held-out data but is worse on the religion dataset
results.metric: accuracy original classifier on religion set
results.setup: SVM RBF trained on 20 newsgroups, Christianity vs Atheism; cleaned classifier 69.0%; test accuracy on 20 newsgroups split 94.0% and 88.6%
results.quote: The original classiﬁer achieves an accuracy score of 57.3% on the religion dataset, while the “cleaned” classiﬁer achieves a score of 69.0%.

results.claim: LIME recovers over 90% of the gold features of interpretable classifiers
results.setup: Sparse LR and decision tree limited to 10 features, books and DVDs, K=10, N=15,000; LIME 92.1/97.0 books, 90.2/97.8 DVDs; parzen 72.8/78.9 and 60.8/80.6; greedy 64.3/37.0 and 63.4/47.6
results.quote: LIME consistently provides > 90% recall for both classiﬁers on both datasets

results.claim: LIME gives highest F1 of trustworthiness for simulated users
results.setup: 25% of features randomly untrustworthy, 100 runs, books and DVDs, LR/NN/RF/SVM; LIME 91.8 to 96.7, parzen 81.7 to 94.3, greedy 45.0 to 58.1, random 14.2 to 14.8
results.quote: all results are signiﬁcant at p = 0.01
results.table: Table 1, row LIME, column Books SVM

results.claim: Crowd workers improved a classifier by removing words with SP-LIME better than RP-LIME
results.setup: B=10 instances, K=10 words, 10 initial subjects then 5 per classifier per round; 250 classifiers after 3 rounds; accuracy shown only in Fig 10
results.quote: Each subject took an average of 3.6 minutes per round of cleaning, resulting in just under 11 minutes

results.claim: SP removed more words per path than RP
results.setup: Same as above; RP 157; 174 of 200 chosen by at least half the users, 68 by all
results.quote: Each path had on average 200 words removed with SP, and 157 with RP

results.claim: Explanations expose spurious features behind a 94% accurate SVM
results.setup: RBF SVM on unigrams, Christianity vs Atheism subset of 20 newsgroups; word Posting in 22% of training examples, 99% of them Atheism
results.quote: Although this classiﬁer achieves 94% held-out accuracy

results.claim: Explaining a random forest is fast
results.setup: RF with 1000 trees, scikit-learn, laptop, N=5000, no GPU or parallelisation; Inception about 10 minutes per prediction
results.quote: takes under 3 seconds without any optimizations

results.claim: Submodular pick greedy gives constant-factor guarantee
results.quote: a constant-factor approximation guarantee of 1−1/e to the optimum

results.claim: SP-LIME best identifies the better of two classifiers in simulation, strongest when few instances shown
results.setup: Pairs of 30-tree random forests with validation accuracy within 0.1% and test accuracy differing by at least 5%, 10 artificial noisy features; curves in Fig 8 only

limits: Experiments are on text and images only; no tabular experiment (the flu example in Fig 1 is an illustration).
Authors concede a highly non-linear model locally may have no faithful linear explanation, and some behaviours (sepia retro) are not expressible in super-pixels.
Local fidelity does not imply global fidelity.
Authors call the Husky vs Wolf sample small; before/after design with no control group is the reader's observation.
Trust simulation uses artificially selected untrustworthy features, which authors acknowledge.

Stability across sampling seeds and choice of N and sigma are not studied; authors leave theoretical properties like the appropriate number of samples to future work; robustness to sampling noise is asserted.
The pick step for images is not addressed; K is constant, not varied.
Only sparse linear explanations were tested with users; the framework allows other families as future work.
Fig 9 and Fig 10 numbers are bar labels or charts only; no significance tests for the human studies.

terms.definition: an explanation must correspond to how the model behaves in the vicinity of the instance being predicted
a representation understandable to humans regardless of the actual features used by the model, e.g. binary word presence or super-pixel presence
greedy selection of B instances maximising the weighted coverage of globally important explanation features
